body:
Why hydropower has environmental effects

Hydropower can generate electricity without burning fossil fuels at the generating plant. However, constructing dams, creating reservoirs and changing river flows can affect natural ecosystems and human settlements.

The environmental consequences depend on the project's scale, location and operation. A large reservoir may submerge extensive land, while a run-of-river project may create a smaller flooded area but still disturb a river reach through diversion.

Effects on river flow and aquatic ecosystems

Changes in downstream flow

River ecosystems are adapted to natural patterns of water movement, including seasonal high and low flows. A dam or diversion may alter the volume, timing and speed of downstream water flow.

For example, if a run-of-river project diverts water through a channel and returns it some distance downstream, the intervening stretch of river may receive less water. Reservoir releases may also change natural seasonal patterns.

Environmental flows are water releases or flow conditions intended to sustain river ecosystems and the communities that depend on them. Maintaining appropriate flows is one way to reduce damage caused by altered river conditions.

Fish migration and aquatic habitats

Dams and barriers may obstruct the movement of fish between feeding, breeding and other habitats. Some fish species need to move along rivers to complete their life cycles.

Measures such as suitable fish-passage arrangements, carefully managed water releases and habitat protection can reduce certain impacts. Their success depends on local fish species, river conditions and appropriate operation.

Sediment movement

Rivers naturally carry sand, silt and other sediments. When water slows in a reservoir, part of this material may settle at the bottom.

This can create 2 related problems:

  • Inside the reservoir: Sediment accumulation can reduce storage capacity over time.
  • Downstream: Reduced sediment transport can affect riverbeds, banks, floodplains and habitats that depend on natural sediment movement.

Reservoir management and sediment-management measures may help reduce these effects, but they cannot make every altered river behave exactly as it did before the dam was built.

Land submergence and displacement

Creating a large reservoir may submerge forests, agricultural land, villages, culturally important places and natural habitats. People who lose homes, farmland or access to resources may need relocation and rehabilitation.

Displacement means that people must leave an area affected by a project. Rehabilitation and resettlement involve measures intended to help affected people establish homes, livelihoods and access to essential services after displacement.

Compensation alone may not fully replace a person's livelihood, community relationships or access to traditional resources. Therefore, the effects on affected communities need to be considered alongside the project's wider benefits.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan

The Narmada Bachao Andolan became associated with opposition to the environmental and social consequences of major dam construction in the Narmada basin, including concerns relating to the Sardar Sarovar Project.

It drew attention to questions of land submergence, displacement, rehabilitation and the distribution of development benefits and costs. Its relevance to this topic is the distinction between a project's intended public benefits and the actual burdens experienced by some affected communities.

Reduced combustion emissions do not imply zero environmental impact. The ecological and social effects of hydropower must be assessed according to the particular river, reservoir, affected habitats and communities.

Dam safety and flood-related risks

A dam must safely withstand the forces of stored and flowing water. Possible hazards include structural problems, seepage, extreme flood inflows, malfunctioning equipment and unsafe or poorly communicated water releases.

A spillway allows water to pass through or over a designated release structure when necessary. Proper inspection, monitoring, reservoir operation, flood forecasting and communication with downstream communities are important to dam safety.

Dam safety also concerns the population living downstream. Even a technically sound dam may create a serious emergency if large releases are not properly managed or timely warnings are not provided.

Dam Safety Act, 2021

India's Dam Safety Act, 2021 came into force on 30 December 2021. It establishes a framework for surveillance, inspection, operation and maintenance of specified dams.

The Act applies to specified dams, including dams more than 15 m high and certain dams between 10 m and 15 m high that satisfy at least 1 statutory condition: crest length of at least 500 m; reservoir capacity of at least 1 million cubic metres; maximum flood discharge of at least 2,000 cubic metres per second; specially difficult foundation problems; or unusual design.

The framework includes the following institutions:

InstitutionLevelBroad role
National Committee on Dam SafetyNationalDam-safety policy and recommendations.
National Dam Safety AuthorityNationalImplementation and regulatory oversight.
State Committee on Dam SafetyStateState-level oversight and coordination.
State Dam Safety OrganisationStateSurveillance, inspection and compliance work.

Important safety measures include regular inspections, monitoring of dam conditions, assessment of risks, emergency action plans and early-warning arrangements. The Act requires pre-monsoon and post-monsoon inspections of specified dams through the dam owner's dam-safety unit.

Balancing benefits and impacts

Hydropower development involves a balance between electricity generation, water supply, flood management, river health and the rights and livelihoods of affected people.

It is inaccurate to treat every hydropower project as equally damaging. A small diversion, a large storage reservoir and a pumped-storage project may have different ecological and social effects. Each requires assessment based on its actual location and operation.

Prelims focus

  • Hydropower projects can alter downstream flow, sediment movement and fish migration.
  • Reservoir sedimentation can reduce storage capacity.
  • Large reservoirs may cause land submergence and displacement.
  • Narmada Bachao Andolan is associated with environmental, displacement and rehabilitation concerns in the Narmada basin.
  • The Dam Safety Act, 2021 came into force on 30 December 2021.
  • Trap: Renewable hydropower is not automatically free from ecological or social impacts.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary India–II, Class 10 Geography, Chapter 3, Water Resources, pp. 26–29; U.S. Geological Survey, Dams and Rivers: A Primer on the Downstream Effects of Dams, Circular 1126, revised 2000, overview; U.S. Geological Survey, Hydroelectric Power Water Use, section Hydropower and the Environment; Central Water Commission, Guidelines for Maintaining Longitudinal Connectivity Through Dams, sections on environmental flows, sediment and fish passage; Ministry of Jal Shakti, Press Information Bureau, Dam Rehabilitation and Improvement Project Phase-II, 30 March 2026, and Implementation of Dam Safety Act, 2021; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Hydropower Impacts: River Ecology, Displacement and Dam Safety

body:
What wind and hydropower have in common

Wind and conventional hydropower both use naturally replenished resources and both can produce electricity by turning a turbine connected to a generator. Their resources, operating conditions and environmental effects are different.

A wind turbine extracts energy from moving air. A hydroelectric turbine extracts energy from moving water. In both cases, the rotating turbine provides mechanical energy to a generator.

The presence of a turbine does not mean the original energy source is the same. The term turbine identifies a rotating energy-conversion machine, not the natural resource driving it.

One comparison across the main technologies

TechnologyEnergy resourceStorage arrangementKey operating limit
Wind powerKinetic energy of moving air.No inherent energy storage in a normal turbine.Changing wind speed and direction.
Run-of-river hydroEnergy of naturally flowing water.Little storage, sometimes limited pondage.Incoming river flow.
Reservoir hydroEnergy of stored or flowing river water.Water retained in a reservoir.Stored water, inflow and release obligations.
Pumped-storage hydroPreviously supplied electricity stored as elevated water.Water moved between 2 reservoirs.Available stored energy and pumping losses.

Renewable resource and energy storage are not identical

Renewable-energy generation uses naturally replenished flows such as wind or river water. Energy storage retains energy that has already been supplied so that it can be used later.

Conventional reservoir hydropower can perform both generation and water-storage functions because the naturally supplied river water can be held before passing through a turbine.

Pumped-storage hydropower has a different central purpose. It consumes electricity to raise water and later recovers part of that electricity through generation. It therefore helps shift energy between periods of supply and demand.

Storage hydropower stores water from natural inflow; pumped-storage hydropower uses electricity to raise water. Both may release elevated water through turbines, but they do not have the same energy balance.

How the two resources can complement each other

Wind generation may rise or fall with atmospheric conditions. Hydropower plants with suitable reservoir storage can sometimes adjust generation more readily than run-of-river plants, provided sufficient water is available and other water-use requirements are respected.

Pumped-storage systems can use electricity available during periods of renewable-energy surplus to move water into an upper reservoir. Later, the stored water can be released to generate electricity when it is more useful.

This relationship does not make wind generation constant. It provides a way to manage some of its variability. Similarly, storage does not remove the effects of drought, ecological constraints or energy losses.

Distinctions that prevent common MCQ errors

  • Wind resource versus wind output: A windy region may have high assessed potential, but generation depends on installed turbines and actual conditions.
  • Strong wind versus maximum turbine output: A turbine regulates its power and may shut down during excessively strong winds.
  • Onshore versus offshore: These identify installation locations, not different basic methods of converting wind energy.
  • Head versus discharge: Head concerns the useful height difference; discharge concerns the amount of water flowing per unit time.
  • Run-of-river versus reservoir: Run-of-river chiefly follows river inflow, while reservoir storage can shift some water use over time.
  • Storage versus pumped storage: The first can retain naturally supplied river water; the second stores electricity through pumping.
  • Renewable versus impact-free: Wind and hydropower can both affect ecosystems and communities.

One-glance classification

The most useful way to classify a system is to identify what supplies its energy, how the turbine is driven, whether energy or water can be stored and what limits its operation.

A wind farm relies on atmospheric movement. Run-of-river hydropower mainly relies on natural river discharge. Reservoir hydropower can retain water and regulate its release. Pumped-storage hydropower uses electricity to raise water and recover part of that energy later.

Prelims focus

  • Wind turbines use kinetic energy of air; hydropower turbines use energy of moving water.
  • The generator converts turbine rotation into electrical energy in both technologies.
  • Run-of-river hydropower has limited storage compared with reservoir-based hydropower.
  • Pumped-storage hydropower is chiefly an energy-storage technology and requires electricity for pumping.
  • Gujarat is relevant to both technologies through wind-resource development and multipurpose projects such as Sardar Sarovar and Ukai.
  • Trap: A project being renewable does not prove that its output is constant or that it has no environmental impact.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, pp. 32–34; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, pp. 82–83; U.S. Department of Energy, How Do Wind Turbines Work?, Types of Hydropower Plants and Pumped Storage Hydropower; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Annual Report 2024–25, Chapter 4; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
